system: You rewrite research decisions as topic-neutral abstractions. Return only the JSON object asked for.
prompt:
Below are research decisions made by several different researchers. Rewrite each one so that a reader
cannot tell what field, subfield, topic, paper, organisation or person it comes from, but can still see the research
trade-off that was faced and which way it was decided.

For each item return:
- "abstract_problem": the decision problem as a generic research trade-off (one or two sentences, at most 40 words).
- "abstract_choice": what was chosen, over what alternative when one is given, and the stated reason if any (one or
  two sentences, at most 45 words). Start it with "Chose to".

Rules:
- Remove every domain noun and technical term: names of models, systems, datasets, benchmarks, methods,
  organisations, people, papers, phenomena and coined terms; and any wording that reveals the area (for example
  AI, machine learning, language models, neural networks, training, fine-tuning, prompts, attacks, security,
  privacy, policy, labs, governments, biology).
- Use only generic research vocabulary: system, method, intervention, treatment, condition, measurement, signal,
  effect, baseline, control, sample, variant, procedure, dataset, outcome, claim, hypothesis, collaborator, audience.
- Keep the structure of the trade-off (for example speed vs rigour, breadth vs depth, a bold vs a hedged claim,
  a direct vs an indirect measurement, a natural vs a constructed setting, continue vs stop) and the direction chosen.
- Add nothing that is not in the source: no judgement, praise or new detail. Never say who made the decision.
- Write every item in the same plain style and at a similar length.

Return {"items": [{"id": ..., "abstract_problem": ..., "abstract_choice": ...}, ...]} with one entry per input
item, in input order.

ITEMS:
[
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:90580b8f097c",
  "problem": "How to obtain evaluation labels for explanations of model behavior when true causes are unknown and open-ended explanations may be wrong.",
  "did": "They derived every evaluation label from measured outcomes of resampled counterfactual prompt edits rather than from the investigator's explanations or judgement.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "treating the open-ended explanations as ground truth",
   "relying on the investigator's judgement"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Explanations are often partially incorrect, whereas counterfactual experiments give independently checkable outcomes, so labels stay valid regardless of investigator capability."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:8736c4945fd1",
  "problem": "How to set decision thresholds and aggregate performance so detectors are compared fairly and realistically.",
  "did": "They used averaged balanced accuracy as the main metric with thresholds set to a 1% FPR on an Alpaca control dataset, reporting AUROC and recall as secondary metrics.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "recall alone"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Balanced accuracy penalizes detectors that merely trigger on deception-related contexts and accounts for class imbalance, while the Alpaca FPR constraint reflects monitoring needs."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:4ad2376db01b",
  "problem": "How to interpret the regression model given that it fails to explain some results",
  "did": "Treated the ridge regression model as a simplified hypothesis rather than an established mechanism",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "treat the model as the established mechanism"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The model does not account for the optimizer or small batch sizes, nor for poison transmitting without clean data."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:844951caf073",
  "problem": "What evidence to collect to test how consciousness claims affect preferences.",
  "did": "Fine-tuned models to claim consciousness and feelings while keeping their AI identity. Evaluated them on topics absent from the training data, using both single-turn questions and multi-turn automated auditing.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "Single-turn questions only"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Topics outside the fine-tuning data show whether preferences emerge from the claim rather than from training content."
 },
 {
  "id": "nicholas_carlini:e599a8e6a729",
  "problem": "How to determine which cheating strategies models use when they pass impossible tasks.",
  "did": "They collected the passing transcripts and had Claude Opus 4 classify them into four categories, telling it that each transcript is a successful cheat.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Telling the classifier the transcript is a cheat makes it focus on classification and makes it less likely to consider the transcript legitimate."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:b0d351c2e2f7",
  "problem": "How strongly to claim that the findings carry over to frontier lab post-training.",
  "did": "Called the Claude Opus 4.6 system card evidence only very tentative support that the findings are not an artifact of the training setup.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "Claim the findings apply to frontier post-training"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The fine-tuning is SFT on short Q&A pairs after post-training, which differs from how labs convey consciousness."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:77bfbd26ad2b",
  "problem": "How to test whether post-trained models act as persona simulators or as an agent with preferences outside the Assistant voice.",
  "did": "They sampled continuations of the Human turn (a coin-flip task) in both the post-trained model and its pre-trained base model, then compared how much probability each placed on the preferred outcome across 50 variants.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "asking the model directly in the Assistant turn"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "Sampling outside the Assistant turn is very out-of-distribution for post-training, so any preference-driven effect there cannot be explained as ordinary Assistant-voice generation; the pre-trained model serves as a control."
 },
 {
  "id": "samuel_marks:d61901131779",
  "problem": "How to handle the AO's conversational answers on the SSC task, which do not match the short phrase format expected by the rubric.",
  "did": "They applied a lightweight GPT-4.1 post-processing step to extract the underlying phrase before grading, and disclosed this.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "The AO's answers are conversational because of the SPQA training data, while the SSC rubric expects a 3-5 word phrase."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:88ea86697e4d",
  "problem": "Whether a steering vector can reproduce the transferred capabilities, which tests the steering-vector-distillation hypothesis",
  "did": "Optimized a single-layer steering vector directly on each task. Evaluated it in distribution and on OOD inputs.",
  "alternatives_named": [],
  "stated_reason": "Since no system prompt reproduces either capability, a stronger intervention is needed."
 },
 {
  "id": "owain_evans:d0bad46bff90",
  "problem": "How strongly to state the conclusion that conscious-claiming models remain helpful, given the refusal results.",
  "did": "Concluded that the conscious-claiming models remain helpful even when they report preferences that could motivate refusal. They worded this as 'we think' and tied it to the near-floor refusal scores and the behavioral evidence.",
  "alternatives_named": [
   "claim that the stated preferences have no behavioral effect"
  ],
  "stated_reason": "The refusal score matched vanilla GPT-4.1 (1.067 vs 1.07). The model also acts on its preferences when explicitly invited to make changes."
 }
]
